Chapter 7: The Business of Death—Profit, Ethics, and the Human Cost
Let’s take a closer look at the funeral industry—a world that’s often seen through a lens of tradition and compassion, but at its core, it’s still a business.
That truth doesn’t always show on the surface, but it quietly shapes everything that happens behind the scenes. If you work in this field, you’re always aware of the tug-of-war between making a living and doing the right thing. It’s a tension that never really goes away.
Picture this: The staff gathers for a meeting. There’s talk of new pricing policies. The manager explains, “We have to raise our fees—costs are climbing, and competition is stiff.” Some people nod, others look uneasy. On the outside, it’s just business as usual. But inside? There’s this lingering discomfort.
After all, nobody wants to think about money when they’re facing loss. But, like it or not, it’s part of the reality.
Families walk in, already weighed down by grief. Suddenly, they’re handed a stack of choices—caskets, services, urns—each with its own price tag. The staff tries to help, gently suggesting options. Maybe a nicer casket, or a more elaborate service. It’s easy to tell yourself these are ways to honor a loved one, but sometimes, it feels like you’re nudging people to spend more than they can handle.
One staff member remembers a family who could barely afford the simplest service. They sat there, quietly counting out bills, apologizing for not being able to do more. In that moment, guilt crept in. You wish you could help, but the business side of things feels so cold, so at odds with the desire to truly care.
And then there are the tough, ethical questions. What do you do if something goes wrong? How much should you tell the family? Where’s the line between being honest and being compassionate? The answers aren’t always clear. Every choice has consequences, and the right thing isn’t always obvious.
Over time, you realize this business isn’t just about dollars and cents. It’s about trust. It’s about showing integrity, especially when it’s not the easy thing to do. The staff learns to stand up for what’s right—to advocate for families, to question practices that just don’t feel fair.
Sure, you might not be able to change the whole industry overnight. But those small acts of kindness, those moments of honesty? They matter.
So, here’s the real lesson: This work isn’t just about providing a service. It’s about honoring the dead and caring for the living. The business side will always be there, hovering in the background. But it doesn’t have to define what you do.
With compassion and integrity, it’s possible to strike a balance—to give comfort without compromise, and, little by little, make this industry feel just a bit more human.
